questions.q: According to the chapter, an element of Nature can be called a resource only when it meets three conditions. Which set of conditions is it?
o: It is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable
It is renewable, plentiful and evenly spread across every part of the country
It is essential for life, useful for materials and a source of energy
It is found on land, owned by some person and sold in a market for money
questions.a: It must be technologically accessible, and its exploitation must be economically feasible and culturally acceptable.

questions.q: Which of these is the chapter's meaning of 'natural resources'?
o: Materials and substances that occur in Nature and are valuable to humans
All life and non-life forms in the environment, whether used or not
Goods that humans make in factories out of raw materials from mines
Only those things in Nature that will never run out, however much we use
questions.a: Natural resources are materials and substances that occur in Nature and are valuable to humans.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Trees standing in a forest are part of Nature even before anyone uses them.
Reason (R): Nature means the totality of life and non-life forms that are part of our environment but have not been created by humans.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: trees exist independently of humans and were not created by them, so they are part of Nature whether or not anyone uses them.

questions.q: True or False? 'In this chapter, the word exploitation has a negative meaning: the harmful misuse of Nature.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The word usually has a negative connotation, but in this chapter it simply means the extraction, utilisation and consumption of natural resources.
s: States the verdict: False
Gives the chapter's meaning: extraction, utilisation and consumption of natural resources, with no negative sense here

questions.q: (a) Give the chapter's example of how a tree comes to be seen as a resource. (b) Name two of the 'not-so-obvious' treasures of the Earth that the chapter says humans have learnt to use.
questions.a: (a) Trees exist independently of humans; when we cut them and convert their wood into furniture, we see the trees as a resource. (b) Any two of: coal, petroleum, precious stones, metal ores, timber.
s: (a) Cutting trees and converting the wood into furniture makes us see trees as a resource
(b) Names two of coal, petroleum, precious stones, metal ores, timber

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) What does the chapter mean by 'Nature'?
(b) Give one reason, from the chapter, why petroleum deep under the ocean might not be a resource.
(c) Give the chapter's example of exploitation that is culturally unacceptable.
questions.a: (a) The totality of life and non-life forms that are part of our environment but have not been created by humans. (b) We may not have the technology to reach it, or the cost of extracting it may be too high. (c) Cutting trees in sacred groves.
s: (a) Life and non-life forms of the environment not created by humans
(b) No technology to reach it, or extraction cost too high
(c) Cutting trees in sacred groves

questions.q: Beside a village in Bihar is a mound of fine clay that is easy to dig with ordinary spades, and potters in the nearby town would pay well for it. But the mound surrounds an old shrine of the village deity, and the villagers do not allow any digging there. A trader says, 'The clay is easy to reach and profitable, so it is already a resource.' Is the trader right? Give reasons using the chapter's conditions.
questions.a: No. The clay meets two conditions: it is technologically accessible (ordinary spades can dig it) and its exploitation is economically feasible (potters would pay well). But digging it is not culturally acceptable, because the villagers hold the shrine sacred and forbid it, just as the chapter says cutting trees in sacred groves is unacceptable. All three conditions must hold, so for now the clay is not a resource.
s: Shows the clay is technologically accessible and economically feasible, with the evidence from the situation
Shows it fails cultural acceptability because the villagers hold the site sacred, like a sacred grove
Verdict: the trader is wrong, because all three conditions must hold

questions.q:
The chapter notes that in many indigenous traditions Nature is considered sacred, a nurturer and nourisher. A student argues: 'A community that treats Nature as sacred cannot use anything from Nature as a resource.' Evaluate this argument.
(a) Which of the chapter's three conditions for a resource does such a belief affect directly?
(b) Give the chapter's example of exploitation that is culturally unacceptable.
(c) Explain why the timber in such a place is not a resource even if machines can reach it and it would sell well.
(d) Using a practice the chapter shows, such as gentle ploughing, show that a community can respect Nature and still use it.
(e) Give your verdict on the student's argument.
questions.a: (a) Cultural acceptability. (b) Cutting trees in sacred groves. (c) All three conditions must hold; if cutting is culturally unacceptable, being reachable and profitable is not enough. (d) Gentle ploughing causes minimal disturbance to the underground ecosystem and retains soil moisture, so the community grows food from the soil while caring for it. (e) The argument goes too far: in such traditions Nature is a nurturer and nourisher, so people do take from it, in respectful ways; what the belief rules out is exploitation the community finds unacceptable, such as cutting a sacred grove.
s: (a) Names cultural acceptability
(b) Cutting trees in sacred groves
(c) Explains all three conditions must hold, so access and profit are not enough
(d) Uses gentle ploughing (minimal disturbance, retains soil moisture) to show respectful use
(e) Verdict: the argument goes too far; Nature as nurturer and nourisher is still used, only unacceptable exploitation is ruled out

questions.q:
Students of a school in Dhanbad visit a mining museum. The guide explains: 'Long ago, people knew there was coal deep under this area, but their tools could not reach it. Today machines can reach it. In Block P the coal can be reached and nobody objects to mining it, but digging out one tonne costs Rs 4,000 and a tonne sells for only Rs 3,000. Block Q lies under a hill with a temple that the local people hold sacred, and they oppose any mining there.'
(a) Which condition for a resource did the deep coal fail long ago?
(b) Which condition does Block P fail? Show it with the figures.
(c) Which condition does Block Q fail?
(d) If the selling price rose to Rs 4,500 a tonne, would the coal of Block P become a resource? Explain.
questions.a: (a) It was not technologically accessible. (b) It is not economically feasible: digging a tonne costs Rs 4,000 but it sells for Rs 3,000, a loss of Rs 1,000 a tonne. (c) It is not culturally acceptable, because the people hold the temple hill sacred. (d) Yes: the price would then be Rs 500 a tonne more than the cost, so mining becomes economically feasible; the coal is already reachable and nobody objects, so all three conditions would hold.
s: (a) Not technologically accessible
(b) Not economically feasible: cost Rs 4,000 against price Rs 3,000, a loss of Rs 1,000 a tonne
(c) Not culturally acceptable (sacred temple hill)
(d) Yes: Rs 500 a tonne above cost, so all three conditions hold

questions.q: According to the chapter, why do we give names to the categories we make?
o: So that a whole set can be referred to in a word or short phrase
So that every object stays in one single group for all time
So that we can count exactly how many resources a country has
So that only scientists can tell which group a thing belongs to
questions.a: Names let us refer to a whole set of ideas or things with just one word or a short phrase, so we need not describe them every time.

questions.q: A farming family in Kutch uses a windmill to pump water from a well. The family drinks the water and also uses it to grow millet for its meals. Which of the chapter's use-based groups appear in this situation?
o: Resources for energy and resources essential for life
Resources for materials and resources for energy
Resources essential for life only
Resources for materials and resources essential for life
questions.a: The wind is a resource for energy, while the drinking water and the food grown from the soil are resources essential for life.

questions.q:
Match each term or example in Column A with what fits it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Criteria  2. Category  3. A piece of wood carved into a statuette  4. Sunlight turned into electricity
Column B: a. a named group, so that a whole set can be referred to in a word or a short phrase  b. a resource for energy  c. the shared characteristics used to sort ideas or things  d. a resource for materials
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b: criteria are the shared characteristics used to sort, a category is a named group, the carved wood is a resource for materials and sunlight made into electricity is a resource for energy.

questions.q: Name the three groups into which the chapter sorts natural resources by their use, and give one example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: Resources essential for life, such as air, water or food from the soil; resources for materials, such as wood, marble, coal or gold; and resources for energy, such as coal, water, petroleum, natural gas, sunlight or wind.
s: Names the three groups: essential for life, for materials, for energy
Gives a correct chapter example for each group

questions.q: (a) The chapter names some natural resources that we cannot make ourselves. Name them and the use-based group they belong to. (b) Using (a), explain why a village whose only pond is poisoned by waste faces a threat to life itself, not just an inconvenience.
questions.a: (a) The air we breathe, the water we drink and the soil that gives us food; they are resources essential for life. (b) The pond's water is a resource essential for life: life cannot exist without it, and the villagers cannot make new water for themselves, so losing it endangers their lives, not just their comfort.
s: (a) Air, water and soil; resources essential for life
(b) Life cannot exist without the water and humans cannot make it, so its loss threatens life

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) What does the chapter call the shared characteristics we use when we categorise ideas or things?
(b) Which simple example of categories, learnt in earlier classes, does the chapter give?
(c) State the first criterion the chapter uses to categorise natural resources.
questions.a: (a) Criteria. (b) Living and non-living things. (c) The uses we put them to, which gives the groups essential for life, for materials and for energy.
s: (a) Criteria
(b) Living and non-living things
(c) The uses we put them to (life, materials, energy)

questions.q: Ishita says: 'A wooden chair made in a factory is itself a natural resource, because it came from a tree.' Is she right? Give reasons using the chapter's meaning of Nature and of natural resources.
questions.a: Partly. She is right that the chair traces back to Nature: the chapter says everything around us leads back to Nature at some point, and the wood came from a tree, which is a resource for materials. But the chair itself is not a natural resource: natural resources are materials and substances that occur in Nature, and Nature means what has not been created by humans, while the chair is an object humans made out of Nature's gift. The wood is the natural resource; the chair is a product made from it.
s: Agrees the chair traces back to Nature and the wood is a resource for materials
Explains the chair is made by humans, so it does not occur in Nature and is not a natural resource
Verdict: partly right; the wood, not the chair, is the natural resource

questions.q:
A school in Nagpur is setting up a 'Resources Corner'. The students list eight things the school uses: drinking water from its well, rice grown in the school garden, teak wood for the benches, sunlight falling on rooftop solar panels, marble for the entrance steps, natural gas for the canteen stove, the air in the classrooms, and gold used to coat a trophy. Using the chapter's use-based groups:
(a) List the items that are resources essential for life.
(b) List the items that are resources for materials.
(c) List the items that are resources for energy.
(d) The chapter calls this grouping only one of the ways to categorise natural resources. Name the second way it gives.
questions.a: (a) The drinking water, the rice grown in the garden (food from the soil) and the air. (b) The teak wood, the marble and the gold. (c) The sunlight on the solar panels and the natural gas for the stove. (d) Whether the resources are renewable or non-renewable.
s: (a) Water, rice and air as resources essential for life
(b) Teak wood, marble and gold as resources for materials
(c) Sunlight and natural gas as resources for energy
(d) Renewable versus non-renewable

questions.q: What does the chapter mean by 'restoration'?
o: Returning something damaged to its original healthy state
Nature's ability to create new life and the conditions for thriving
Taking timber from a forest faster than new trees can grow
Turning the waste from factories into food for other lifeforms
questions.a: Restoration is the process of returning something to its original healthy state if it has been degraded or damaged.

questions.q: A forest stands upstream of a small town in Himachal Pradesh. Which of these is an ecosystem service, not just an ecosystem function?
o: The townspeople get clean water because the forest filters it
The forest provides a habitat for animals
The forest's roots prevent soil erosion on the slopes
The forest naturally filters the water that flows through it
questions.a: Clean water for the townspeople is an ecosystem service: it is the benefit humans receive from the forest's natural function of filtering water.

questions.q:
Read the statements about how Nature heals and renews itself.
I. Regeneration goes beyond restoration: it is Nature's ability to create new life and the conditions for thriving.
II. The chapter's examples of a cut on the skin healing and a forest recovering after a wildfire show regeneration going beyond restoration.
III. Planting the types of trees that originally grew in an area restores the ecosystem, enabling life to return.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the healing cut and the forest recovering after a wildfire are the chapter's examples of restoration, a return to an earlier healthy state.

questions.q: True or False? 'An ecosystem function goes on in Nature whether or not humans gain anything from it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Ecosystem functions are Nature's own ways of working, such as a forest filtering water or providing habitat for animals; they are called ecosystem services only when humans benefit from them.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that functions are Nature's inherent ways of working and are called services only when humans benefit

questions.q: (a) What happens to a tree that falls in a forest, according to the chapter? (b) Why does this show that Nature works in cycles where there is no waste?
questions.a: (a) It decomposes as bacteria, fungi and insects feed on it, and it becomes part of the soil, enriching it. (b) Nothing is left over: the fallen tree feeds other living things and the soil, new trees and plants grow from seeds in that soil, and when some of them fall the cycle starts again.
s: (a) Decomposed by bacteria, fungi and insects; becomes part of the soil and enriches it
(b) The tree becomes food and soil for new life, so nothing is wasted and the cycle repeats

questions.q:
A housing society in Indore has 12 mature trees in its park. Use the chapter's figures: a mature tree produces about 275 litres of oxygen a day, and a person needs about 350 litres a day.
(a) About how many litres of oxygen do the 12 trees produce in a day?
(b) The full daily need of how many people does this cover? Give a whole number.
(c) The chapter says both figures can vary. Give one thing each figure depends on.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 275 = 3,300 litres. (b) 3,300 / 350 = about 9.4, so the full daily need of 9 people. (c) A tree's output varies with the type of tree; a person's need varies with the person's activity, height and weight.
s: (a) 3,300 litres a day
(b) About 9.4, so 9 people's full daily need
(c) Type of tree; the person's activity, height or weight

questions.q: Compare what happens to a tree that falls in a forest with what happens to untreated waste that a factory pours into a river. Explain why one keeps Nature's cycle going and the other breaks it, and state the end result for the river.
questions.a: The fallen tree decomposes as bacteria, fungi and insects feed on it and becomes part of the soil, so it feeds new life and nothing is wasted. The factory waste often cannot decay to become the food of any lifeform, so it is not taken up by Nature's cycle and instead disturbs the cycle of restoration and regeneration. In the end the river can become poisonous and unable to support life.
s: Fallen tree: decomposed by bacteria, fungi and insects, enriches the soil, no waste
Factory waste: cannot decay into food for any lifeform, so it disturbs restoration and regeneration
End result: the river becomes poisonous and cannot support life

questions.q:
Fifteen years ago, a patch of trees beside a school in Ranchi was cleared to build a new block. The school now plans to plant trees on the land that is left. Using the chapter, answer each part in a line or two.
(a) Which types of trees should the school plant so that the ecosystem is restored?
(b) Name two kinds of creatures the chapter says return when such trees provide food and shelter.
(c) Is bringing back the original trees an example of restoration? Give the chapter's meaning of the word.
(d) Years later, one of the trees falls. Name the living things that will help turn it into soil.
(e) Name one ecosystem service the school might receive from the trees.
questions.a: (a) The types of trees that were originally growing there. (b) Birds and squirrels. (c) Yes: restoration is returning something to its original healthy state after it has been degraded or damaged. (d) Bacteria, fungi and insects, which feed on it until it becomes part of the soil. (e) For example, the oxygen the trees produce, which the students and teachers breathe: a natural process that benefits humans.
s: (a) The types of trees originally growing there
(b) Birds and squirrels
(c) Yes, with the meaning: returning to the original healthy state after damage
(d) Bacteria, fungi and insects
(e) A benefit to people from the trees' natural working, such as oxygen

questions.q:
A ward in Pune plans to widen a busy road by cutting 30 of the 50 mature trees that line it. Residents use the chapter's figures: a mature tree produces about 275 litres of oxygen a day and a person needs about 350 litres a day. Birds nest in the trees, and traffic on the road is heavy and slow.
(a) How many litres of oxygen do all 50 trees produce in a day?
(b) How many litres a day would be lost if the 30 trees are cut? This equals the full daily need of about how many people?
(c) For the residents, is the trees' production of oxygen an ecosystem function, an ecosystem service, or both? Explain.
(d) Should the ward cut the 30 trees? Give a decision that weighs both sides, using your figures.
questions.a: (a) 50 x 275 = 13,750 litres a day. (b) 30 x 275 = 8,250 litres a day, which is 8,250 / 350 = about 23.6, so the full daily need of about 23 people. (c) Both: producing oxygen is what trees naturally do (a function), and because the residents benefit from it, it is also an ecosystem service to them. (d) A justified decision either way, for example: cut fewer trees or none, because 8,250 litres of oxygen a day and the birds' nesting places would be lost for many years while new trees grow, even though traffic would move faster; or widen the road but plant at least as many trees of the original kinds nearby, accepting a loss until they mature.
s: (a) 13,750 litres a day
(b) 8,250 litres a day, about 23 people's full daily need
(c) Both: a natural function that becomes a service because residents benefit
(d) A decision that uses the figures and weighs the traffic need against the lost ecosystem services

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter list as a non-renewable resource?
o: Copper
Wind energy
Timber from forests
Energy from flowing water
questions.a: Copper: the chapter lists minerals and metals such as iron, copper and gold as non-renewable resources.

questions.q: A village in Assam cuts 500 bamboo poles a year from its grove, while the grove grows only about 350 new poles a year (illustrative figures). What does the chapter's idea of a renewable resource predict?
o: The grove will slowly be depleted, because more is cut each year than grows back
The grove will last for ever, because bamboo is always a renewable resource
The grove becomes non-renewable only once its poles are sold outside the village
The grove will heal itself, because Nature always restores what is lost
questions.a: The grove will be depleted: 500 poles are cut but only 350 grow back each year, so the natural rhythm of regeneration is disturbed and the renewable resource stops renewing.

questions.q:
Match each resource in Column A with the description in Column B that fits it, according to the chapter.
Column A: 1. Gold  2. Wind energy  3. Coal  4. Timber
Column B: a. renewable only if the forest is allowed to regenerate  b. a fossil fuel; India's reserves may last another 50 years  c. a metal that cannot be replenished at the rate we use it  d. a renewable source of energy
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a: gold is a metal that cannot be replenished as fast as we use it, wind is a renewable energy source, coal is a fossil fuel whose Indian reserves may last about 50 years, and timber stays renewable only if the forest regenerates.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Coal is a non-renewable resource.
Reason (R): The demand for electricity in India has been increasing as the population expands and development work accelerates.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Coal is non-renewable because it was created over long periods and cannot be replenished at the rate we use it; rising demand explains why we must use it judiciously, not why it is non-renewable.

questions.q: State the condition the chapter gives for a renewable resource to remain renewable, and give the chapter's example of what happens when the condition is broken.
questions.a: The natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration must not be disturbed. If we harvest timber faster than the forest can grow trees, we will eventually deplete the forest.
s: States the condition: the natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration must not be disturbed
Gives the timber example: harvesting faster than the forest grows trees depletes it

questions.q: The chapter says India's coal reserves may last another 50 years. (a) A student is 13 years old today. About how old will she be when the reserves run out, at this estimate? (b) What does the chapter say we must do with coal until more sustainable options are widely available, and why does rising demand make this important?
questions.a: (a) About 13 + 50 = 63 years old. (b) We must use the coal we have judiciously; the demand for electricity keeps rising as the population expands and development accelerates, so the pressure on the limited reserves keeps growing.
s: (a) About 63 years old
(b) Use coal judiciously, because demand for electricity keeps rising while the reserves are limited

questions.q: Nisha says: 'Timber and coal can both run out, but for different reasons.' Is she right? Give reasons using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Coal is non-renewable: it was created over long periods and cannot be replenished at the rate we use it, so steady use runs it down; India's reserves may last about 50 years. Timber is renewable, but only while the natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration is not disturbed; it runs out only if we harvest it faster than the forest can grow trees. So both can run out: coal because it cannot be replaced fast enough, timber because of overharvesting.
s: Coal: non-renewable, cannot be replenished at the rate we use it
Timber: renewable but runs out if harvested faster than the forest regrows
Verdict: she is right; the two reasons differ as shown

questions.q:
A school in Jodhpur uses five resources every day: coal burnt at a power station to supply its electricity, petroleum fuel for its bus, sunlight falling on its rooftop solar panels, timber in its wooden benches, and copper in its water pipes.
(a) Sort the five into renewable and non-renewable resources.
(b) For the two energy uses that depend on non-renewables, suggest a renewable substitute named in the chapter.
(c) State the condition under which the timber stays a renewable resource.
(d) Which switch should the school make first? Give a reason using the chapter's advice on non-renewables.
questions.a: (a) Renewable: sunlight and timber. Non-renewable: coal, petroleum and copper. (b) Electricity from the sun or the wind in place of coal power, and a renewable energy source such as solar power in place of petroleum for transport. (c) The forest must not be harvested faster than it can grow trees, so that its natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration is not disturbed. (d) For example, add more solar panels to replace the coal-based electricity first, since the school already uses sunlight and most of India has abundant sunshine; the chapter says we must switch to renewable energy for as many purposes as we can so that non-renewables last until sustainable alternatives are found.
s: (a) Renewable: sunlight, timber; non-renewable: coal, petroleum, copper
(b) A renewable energy source (sun, wind) in place of coal electricity and of petroleum
(c) Timber is not harvested faster than the forest can grow trees
(d) A first switch with a reason from the chapter (stretch non-renewables, switch to renewables for as many purposes as possible)

questions.q:
'A renewable resource stays renewable only as long as humans let it.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
(a) Give the chapter's meaning of renewable resources, with two examples.
(b) State the condition for them to remain renewable.
(c) Explain how timber can stop renewing.
(d) Explain how human actions are threatening the river water used in the plains below the Himalayas.
(e) Explain how the decline of tuna fits the statement.
questions.a: (a) Renewable resources restore and regenerate over time; solar energy, wind energy, energy from flowing water and timber are renewable as long as we manage them sustainably. (b) The natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration must not be disturbed. (c) If we harvest timber faster than the forest can grow trees, the forest is eventually depleted. (d) Fossil-fuel-driven industrialisation and the cutting of forests are among the factors behind rising temperatures; glaciers in some places in the Himalayas are melting faster than precipitation can replace them, which threatens water security for people in the plains who depend on this 'water tower'. (e) Communities traditionally regulated fishing in the spawning season to maintain the fish population, but commercial fishing led to over-fishing, and tuna, which keeps the ocean ecosystem in balance, is on the decline despite agreements to control fishing. In every case human action decides whether the resource keeps renewing.
s: (a) Meaning of renewable resources with two chapter examples
(b) The natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration must not be disturbed
(c) Timber harvested faster than the forest grows depletes it
(d) Rising temperatures from human factors melt Himalayan glaciers faster than precipitation replaces them, threatening water security in the plains
(e) Over-fishing after commercialisation broke the spawning-season practice, so tuna is declining; conclusion that human action decides

questions.q: Some regions that are rich in natural resources experience slower economic growth and development. What do economists call this?
o: The paradox of plenty
The cycle of restoration
Ecosystem services
The Green Revolution
questions.a: Economists call it the 'natural resource curse' or the 'paradox of plenty'.

questions.q: The chapter's example of sharing a river's water across political boundaries is the Kaveri. Among which states and union territory is its water shared?
o: Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry
Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Goa
Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Telangana
Karnataka, Kerala, Goa and Maharashtra
questions.a: The Kaveri's water is shared among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the distribution of natural resources.
I. The chapter notes that many wars have been fought, and are still being fought, to gain control over natural resources.
II. The chapter says that industries set up near natural resources bring only benefits to the people living there.
III. The chapter says that agreements on sharing natural resources are easy to reach between neighbouring countries.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong: the benefits come with costs, such as people being displaced from their homes and sacred places being threatened. Statement III is wrong: the chapter says such agreements between neighbouring countries are not easy.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A country that has plenty of natural resources will always be rich.
Reason (R): Frequently, economies are unable to develop industries that convert their natural resources into products of higher value.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Plenty of natural resources does not guarantee prosperity (the paradox of plenty); R is true, and it is in fact one reason why resource-rich regions can grow slowly.

questions.q: Explain the 'paradox of plenty' in one or two sentences, and state how India has generally avoided it.
questions.a: Having plenty of natural resources does not automatically make a country rich; some resource-rich regions grow more slowly, often because they cannot develop industries that turn the resources into products of higher value. India has generally avoided this curse by investing in the development of such industries to meet its growing needs.
s: Explains that abundant resources do not guarantee prosperity, as economies may fail to build industries that add value
India invested in developing such industries

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) Name any two things that, according to the chapter, the uneven distribution of natural resources shapes.
(b) Why does the sharing of natural resources lead to tensions between states and between countries?
(c) What was needed to keep peace and fair sharing of the Kaveri's water?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: human settlements, trade patterns, international relations, conflicts. (b) Nature does not pay attention to political boundaries, so a resource such as a river crosses them and has to be shared. (c) Negotiations and deft management.
s: (a) Two of settlements, trade patterns, international relations, conflicts
(b) Nature ignores political boundaries
(c) Negotiations and deft management

questions.q: Deepa says: 'Since Nature pays no attention to political boundaries, sharing a river between two Indian states is exactly as hard as sharing one between two countries.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. She is right that, because Nature ignores political boundaries, sharing a river causes tensions both between states and between countries. But the chapter shows that the Kaveri's water was shared among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry through negotiations and deft management, and then says that reaching such agreements between neighbouring countries is 'not easy'. So the chapter does not treat the two as equally hard.
s: Agrees that ignoring political boundaries causes tensions at both levels
Uses the Kaveri: shared among states through negotiations and deft management
Verdict: partly right; the chapter says agreements between neighbouring countries are not easy

questions.q:
A state (illustrative) has large iron-ore deposits in a hilly, forested district where about 200 families live and a hill sacred to them stands. It has two plans. Plan A: dig the ore and sell all of it raw to buyers outside the state. Plan B: also build steel plants in the state that turn the ore into products of higher value.
(a) Which plan risks the 'paradox of plenty'? Explain why.
(b) What has India generally done to avoid this curse?
(c) Give two benefits the chapter says industries near natural resources bring.
(d) Give two costs the chapter warns may come with them.
(e) Recommend a plan, and state one condition you would attach so that the benefits become lasting rather than a temporary windfall.
questions.a: (a) Plan A: selling raw ore earns money without building industries that convert the resource into products of higher value, which is why resource-rich regions can end up with slower growth. (b) India has invested in developing such industries to meet its growing needs. (c) Any two of: employment for local people; townships that grow and expand economic opportunities for others; modern facilities that improve the quality of life. (d) People displaced from their homes; sacred places threatened, leading to conflicts. (e) For example, Plan B, on condition that the families are treated fairly and the sacred hill is left untouched, because the chapter says human knowledge, good governance and strategic planning decide whether resources become lasting benefits or temporary windfalls, and extraction must be balanced with sustainability.
s: (a) Plan A, because no industry converts the ore into products of higher value
(b) India invested in developing such industries
(c) Two benefits: local employment, townships and wider opportunities, modern facilities
(d) Two costs: displacement, threats to sacred places and conflict
(e) A recommendation with a condition linked to knowledge, good governance, planning or sustainability

questions.q:
In 2005 a forest village in Chhattisgarh (illustrative figures) had about 800 people, a primary school and no hospital. Then a mine opened nearby. By 2025 a township of 12,000 people had grown around it, with a hospital and two secondary schools. The mine employs 3,500 workers, of whom 1,400 come from the old village and nearby hamlets. To make room for the mine, 260 families were moved from their homes, and part of a hill the villagers hold sacred was dug away.
(a) What percentage of the mine's workers are local people?
(b) Name two benefits from the case that match what the chapter says such industries bring.
(c) Name two costs from the case that match the chapter's warnings.
(d) Has the mine been good for the original villagers? Give a balanced judgement using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 1,400 / 3,500 x 100 = 40 per cent. (b) Employment for local people, and a township with modern facilities such as a hospital and schools that improve the quality of life. (c) 260 families displaced from their homes, and a sacred hill damaged, which can lead to conflict. (d) Mixed: many villagers gained jobs and access to a hospital and schools, but 60 per cent of the jobs went to people from outside, families lost their homes and a sacred place was harmed, so the benefits came with real short-term and long-term costs.
s: (a) 40 per cent
(b) Local jobs; a township with modern facilities (hospital, schools)
(c) Displacement of 260 families; damage to a sacred hill
(d) A balanced judgement that uses the 40 per cent figure and weighs the benefits against the costs

questions.q: According to the chapter, about how much of the area of Punjab has been classified as 'over-exploited' for groundwater?
o: Almost 80 per cent
Almost 30 per cent
Almost 50 per cent
Almost 15 per cent
questions.a: Almost 80 per cent of the area of Punjab has been classified as over-exploited.

questions.q: A farmer in Punjab gives up a high-yielding paddy variety and returns to a traditional crop that needs less water, but he still gets free power for his pump. According to the chapter's account, which problem could still continue on his farm?
o: Over-pumping of groundwater, because free power encourages it
Glaciers melting faster than precipitation replaces them
Soil damage caused by mulching and multi-cropping
Fine dust settling on his crops and cutting yields
questions.a: Over-pumping of groundwater can continue: the chapter says the supply of free power led to over-pumping, separately from the extra water that high-yielding varieties needed.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with its meaning in Column B, as the chapter uses it.
Column A: 1. Stewardship  2. Biodiversity loss  3. Over-exploited groundwater  4. Soil degradation
Column B: a. the decline in the variety of life on Earth  b. water drawn at a rate much greater than restoration and rejuvenation can make up  c. using resources so that renewables can restore and regenerate and non-renewables are used judiciously  d. damage to soil caused by the improper use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d: stewardship is using resources so renewables regenerate and non-renewables are used judiciously, biodiversity loss is the decline in the variety of life, over-exploited means drawing water much faster than it is restored, and soil degradation comes from improper use of chemicals.

questions.q: (a) Name two strategies the chapter lists for raising groundwater levels. (b) Name two traditional practices that enabled holistic soil management.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: traditional water harvesting, rejuvenating ponds and tanks, cutting down on wasteful consumption of water, processing and reusing water. (b) Any two of: using cow dung and other natural fertilisers, mulching, multi-cropping.
s: (a) Two of water harvesting, rejuvenating ponds and tanks, cutting wasteful use, processing and reusing water
(b) Two of cow dung and natural fertilisers, mulching, multi-cropping

questions.q: Kulwinder's family farms near Bathinda in Punjab. Like many farmers since the 1960s, they grow high-yielding wheat and paddy using chemical fertilisers and pesticides. (a) Using the chapter, explain why these crops made farmers pump more groundwater than before. (b) Name two separate effects on Punjab's groundwater that the chapter reports from this way of farming.
questions.a: (a) The high-yielding varieties needed more water than the traditional seeds, so farmers extracted groundwater to meet the need (and free power led to over-pumping). (b) In a large part of Punjab groundwater has become inaccessible till depths of about 30 metres, and chemicals from the pesticides and fertilisers have dissolved in it, causing health hazards.
s: (a) High-yielding varieties need more water than traditional seeds, met from groundwater
(b) Groundwater inaccessible to about 30 metres; dissolved chemicals causing health hazards

questions.q: The chapter describes this chain for groundwater: water is extracted faster than the water table is replenished, so a deficit builds up, the cost of extraction rises, and finally the water becomes unavailable. Write a short situation set in a growing Indian city that follows this chain step by step, and then name two strategies from the chapter that could break it.
questions.a: Example: In a growing city in Telangana, every new block of flats sinks a borewell, and together they draw more water each year than the rain puts back. The water table falls year after year, so borewells must be drilled deeper and pumping costs rise; at last many borewells run dry and the residents have no groundwater. Strategies: rejuvenate the city's ponds and tanks, harvest rainwater, cut wasteful use, or process and reuse water.
s: Situation shows extraction greater than replenishment, building a deficit
Situation shows the rising cost of extraction and then unavailability
Names two chapter strategies: water harvesting, rejuvenating ponds and tanks, cutting wasteful use, processing and reusing water

questions.q:
Two neighbouring farms in Bijnor, Uttar Pradesh, grow the same crop (illustrative figures, in quintals per acre). Farm A uses chemical fertilisers and pesticides heavily every year; its yields over four years were 30, 28, 25 and 21. Farm B uses cow dung, mulching and multi-cropping; its yields were 22, 23, 24 and 24.
(a) By what percentage did Farm A's yield fall from the first year to the fourth?
(b) What does the chapter say such traditional practices, as used on Farm B, enabled?
(c) Use the chapter to explain the trend on Farm A.
(d) Farm A earned more in the first two years. Which farm's method would you advise for the next twenty years? Justify, using the figures.
questions.a: (a) (30 - 21) / 30 x 100 = 30 per cent. (b) Holistic soil management; traditional farming considered soil to be part of Mother Earth. (c) The improper use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides degrades the soil, so the yields keep falling. (d) Farm B's method: its yield is steady and rising (22 to 24) while Farm A's keeps falling and is already below Farm B's (21 against 24) by the fourth year; Farm A's early lead is short-term, and the chapter says we must learn from traditional practices to prevent further degradation and replenish the soil.
s: (a) A fall of 30 per cent
(b) Holistic soil management
(c) Improper chemical use degrades the soil, so yields fall
(d) Advises Farm B's method using the figures (steady 22 to 24 against a fall to 21) and the long-term view

questions.q:
A farming block in Moga district, Punjab, kept these records (illustrative figures). In 2000 it had 900 tube wells, groundwater stood 12 metres below the ground, and pumping cost a farmer about Rs 6,000 a season. In 2022 it had 1,600 tube wells, the water stood 28 metres down, and pumping cost about Rs 15,000 a season. Most fields grow paddy and wheat, and farm power is free.
(a) By what percentage did the number of tube wells rise from 2000 to 2022?
(b) How many times the 2000 pumping cost is the 2022 cost? Which step in the chapter's groundwater chain does this show?
(c) Using the chapter, give two reasons why groundwater was drawn so heavily in this block.
(d) The panchayat proposes that half the paddy area switch to crops that need less water, though incomes may dip for a few years. Should the block accept? Justify.
questions.a: (a) (1,600 - 900) / 900 x 100 = about 78 per cent. (b) 15,000 / 6,000 = 2.5 times; it shows the higher cost of extraction that follows when the deficit builds up, on the way to the water becoming unavailable. (c) High-yielding paddy and wheat need more water than traditional seeds, and free power led to over-pumping. (d) A justified decision, for example: yes, because the water fell 16 metres in 22 years and costs rose 2.5 times, so carrying on risks the water becoming unavailable; the chapter says food security was ensured for the short term but the long-term consequences take time and effort to heal, so a short dip in income is worth protecting the groundwater. A reasoned 'no' that uses the figures and proposes another way to cut extraction is also acceptable.
s: (a) About 78 per cent
(b) 2.5 times; the rising cost of extraction as the deficit builds
(c) Thirsty high-yielding varieties and free power
(d) A decision that uses the figures and weighs short-term income against long-term water security

questions.q: Which body has created guidelines for cement factories so that their pollution is minimised or eliminated?
o: The Central Pollution Control Board
The International Alliance for Solar Energy
The Auroville Earth Institute
The state government of Sikkim
questions.a: The Central Pollution Control Board.

questions.q: A town council runs its streetlights and water pumps on electricity from a coal-fired power station. Following the chapter's advice on non-renewable resources, which step should it take?
o: Move as many uses as it can to renewable energy such as solar power
Use more coal now while it is cheap, since it may run out anyway
Stop using electricity at once, since coal is non-renewable
Carry on as before, since the coal will last another 50 years
questions.a: It should switch to renewable sources of energy for as many purposes as it can, so that non-renewables like coal last long enough for sustainable alternatives to be found.

questions.q:
Read the statements about sustainable practices described in the chapter.
I. Surapala's Vrikshayurveda was written around the 10th century BCE.
II. India and France launched the International Alliance for Solar Energy in 2015.
III. After Sikkim became a fully organic state, farmers' incomes grew by 20 per cent on average.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: Surapala's Vrikshayurveda dates from around the 10th century CE, not BCE.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When Pema's family in Sikkim first switched to organic farming, their yields dropped.
Reason (R): Organic farming depends on using more chemical fertilisers than before.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The yields dropped at first because the soil was recovering from years of chemical use; organic farming uses compost and natural pest repellents such as neem and garlic, not chemical fertilisers.

questions.q: True or False? 'Cement production pollutes only the air.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Its fine dust enters the lungs of people and animals and settles on plant leaves, decreasing their yields, and cement production also causes soil and water pollution.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the dust also harms lungs and plant yields, and production pollutes soil and water

questions.q: A vegetable grower in Kerala wants to protect her crop from pests without chemical pesticides. (a) Suggest two methods taken from what the chapter says about Vrikshayurveda and the Sikkim farmers. (b) Using the Punjab caselet, give one reason why avoiding chemical pesticides also protects the water her family draws from its well.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: natural pest repellents such as those made from neem and garlic; growing together the plants that should be grown together, as Vrikshayurveda specifies; growing multiple crops across the year. (b) In Punjab, chemicals from pesticides and fertilisers dissolved in the groundwater and caused health hazards, so avoiding them keeps such chemicals out of her well water.
s: (a) Two methods: natural repellents (neem, garlic), plants grown together, multiple crops
(b) Chemicals from pesticides dissolve in groundwater and cause health hazards, as in Punjab

questions.q:
Answer from the chapter's caselet about Pema's family farm in Sikkim.
(a) What two problems did the farm face before the change?
(b) Name the three changes the family made in its farming.
(c) Give two results for Sikkim after it became a 100 per cent organic state in 2016.
questions.a: (a) Declining yields and mounting debts from expensive chemical inputs. (b) They switched to compost, prepared natural pest repellents using neem and garlic, and grew multiple crops across the year. (c) Any two of: local biodiversity flourished, with beneficial insects and birds returning; tourism increased; farmers' incomes grew by 20 per cent on average.
s: (a) Declining yields and debts from expensive chemical inputs
(b) Compost, neem and garlic repellents, multiple crops across the year
(c) Two of: biodiversity flourished, tourism grew, incomes up 20 per cent on average

questions.q:
A school trust in Jaisalmer district must choose how to build a new hostel. Plan X uses ordinary cement concrete. Plan Y uses mud with modern techniques, like the building made by the Auroville Earth Institute, and is built by local workers.
(a) Give three harms that, according to the chapter, the production of cement causes.
(b) What has the Central Pollution Control Board done about this pollution?
(c) Give three features the chapter says new materials made by combining traditional and modern methods have.
(d) A trustee doubts that mud can last. Give one example from the chapter that answers this doubt.
(e) Which plan would you recommend? Justify, naming one point in favour of the other plan.
questions.a: (a) Its fine dust enters the lungs of humans and animals and damages them; it settles on plant leaves and decreases yields; it causes soil and water pollution. (b) It has created guidelines for cement factories so that pollution is minimised or eliminated. (c) Their production is less polluting, they provide local employment, and they are designed keeping in mind the climate of the place. (d) Jaisalmer fort, a mud structure built in the 12th century (later refurbished with sandstone), or the modern mud community building in Auroville. (e) For example Plan Y, because it avoids cement's pollution, gives local workers jobs and is designed for the local climate; a point for Plan X is that cement is the usual material for buildings such as schools and hospitals, and cement factories now have pollution guidelines to follow. Either plan is acceptable with such reasoning.
s: (a) Three harms: lungs, plant yields, soil and water pollution
(b) Guidelines for cement factories to minimise or eliminate pollution
(c) Less polluting production, local employment, suited to the local climate
(d) Jaisalmer fort (12th century mud structure) or the Auroville mud building
(e) A justified recommendation that also names a point for the other plan

questions.q: (a) Which text refers to lokasangraha, and what idea does the word express? (b) Give one example the chapter gives of unfair access to a basic resource.
questions.a: (a) The Bhagavad Gita; lokasangraha is the idea that everyone must transcend personal desires and act for the wellbeing of all. (b) Many areas in cities do not receive an adequate and regular supply of drinking water; or air pollution from industries and excessive use of fossil fuels affects those who are unable to protect themselves.
s: (a) The Bhagavad Gita; acting for the wellbeing of all beyond personal desires
(b) Inadequate drinking water in many city areas, or air pollution hurting those unable to protect themselves
